questions.question: What does DNS stand for?
questions.explanation: DNS stands for Domain Name System — a distributed directory service that maps domain names to IP addresses.

questions.question: What is the primary function of DNS?
options: Mapping domain names to IP addresses
questions.explanation: DNS maps domain names (like www.google.com) to their associated IP addresses so clients can reach the correct servers.

questions.question: At which layer of the OSI model is DNS implemented?
questions.explanation: DNS is an application layer protocol implemented by a hierarchy of name servers.

questions.question: How many logical root name servers exist in the DNS hierarchy?
questions.explanation: There are 13 logical root 'servers' around the world, each replicated by hundreds of physical hosts for fault-tolerance.

questions.question: What does a root name server respond with when queried?
options: The IP address of the requested domain
The address of a TLD name server
The address of the authoritative name server
questions.explanation: Root name servers hold the addresses of TLD name servers. When queried, they respond with the address of the appropriate TLD name server.

questions.question: Which DNS server is the definitive source of truth for a domain's DNS records?
questions.explanation: Authoritative name servers store DNS records for a domain and are the source of truth. They may delegate some records to another authoritative name server.

questions.question: What is the role of a DNS resolver?
options: Store DNS records for a domain
Hold addresses of TLD name servers
Query other DNS servers until the record is found
Assign TTL values to DNS records
questions.explanation: A DNS resolver receives requests from clients (like web browsers) and is responsible for querying other DNS servers until the requested record is found.

questions.question: Who typically hosts DNS resolvers for end users?
questions.explanation: ISPs typically host DNS resolvers, which resolve DNS requests on behalf of hosts on their networks.

questions.question: What mechanism does DNS use to reduce repeated lookups and improve latency?
questions.explanation: DNS caches results with a Time To Live (TTL) expiration period to reduce the number of requests and improve latency.

questions.question: What does TTL stand for in DNS caching?
questions.explanation: TTL stands for Time To Live — the expiration period for a cached DNS record.

questions.question: When a DNS query returns a cached response, it is called a:
questions.explanation: A cached DNS response is a non-authoritative result — it did not originate directly from an authoritative name server.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a layer where DNS caching can occur?
questions.explanation: DNS caching occurs in the browser, OS, organization's local DNS server, and ISP's resolver. It's not standard for domain registrars to maintain a caching layer.

questions.question: A DNS change propagates globally instantly once made.
questions.explanation: DNS changes can take hours to propagate globally because of TTL-based caching at multiple layers. DNS trades strong consistency for high read performance.

questions.question: DNS is a read-heavy system with orders of magnitude more reads than writes.
questions.explanation: DNS is a read-heavy system — trillions of DNS queries are processed every day, vastly outnumbering the number of DNS record updates.

questions.question: Authoritative name servers may delegate some DNS records to another authoritative name server.
questions.explanation: Authoritative name servers are the source of truth for a domain and may delegate some records to another authoritative name server for management purposes.
